messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Rivas, a 59-year-old divorced project manager from a Latin American family, described the trauma as a period when she was taken captive and repeatedly confined in locked rooms, with no clear way out and no sense that anyone would come for her. What stayed with her most was the physical helplessness of it: the press of walls, the sound of a door locking, the ache that ran up her neck each time she was forced to sit still and wait. Since then, even ordinary moments have carried the force of that experience. When she finds herself in a closed office conference room, in a stalled elevator, or simply turning the key to her apartment at night and realizing she is alone behind a locked door, her body reacts before she has time to reason with herself. She becomes instantly on guard inside her own home, unable to settle on the couch or relax in bed, and she starts scanning for what might go wrong. At work, as a project manager, she now avoids taking the lead in meetings held in small rooms with the door shut, and she feels a sharp tightening in her neck when a room feels confining, as if her body remembers the captivity before her mind can catch up.

As the months passed, Marisol came to believe that the event had changed something fundamental about her. She said she used to be happy, but now she felt “always miserable,” and at times even dead inside, as if part of her had gone cold and stayed there. She also found herself repeating the thought that you can never know who will harm you, a belief that made the world seem unsafe in ways she could not turn off. When those thoughts took hold, they made the enclosed spaces and trapped feelings even more potent: a locked room was no longer just uncomfortable, but proof that she could be trapped again; a twinge of neck pain could become a warning that danger was near. Her hopelessness and fear fed back into the moments that frightened her, so that being unable to see an exit or being left alone at home did not merely remind her of the past, but confirmed her sense that harm was still possible and that she would not be protected.

Trying to manage this, Marisol relied on strategies that gave her brief relief but left her more stuck. She told herself, sometimes almost pleadingly, that maybe it had not really happened or had not been as bad as she remembered. Yet the need to dismiss it never held for long, and she would soon find herself dwelling on what she had done wrong, replaying each decision and going over the details again and again, searching for the moment she should have acted differently. Those mental loops did not settle her; instead, they kept the event vivid and unfinished, which made her feel even more on edge. The more she tried to make sense of it, the more convinced she became that she had missed some warning or failed herself somehow, and that belief deepened her misery and the feeling that she was emotionally deadened. Once those thoughts were in place, she was even more alert at home and less able to relax, as if her own mind had become another place where she could not let her guard down. She also noticed that the more exhausted and hypervigilant she felt, the more likely she was to fixate on any sense of confinement or body tension. A closed door, a narrow hallway, or the familiar neck pain could suddenly take on alarming meaning, and she would avoid rooms, routes, and situations that might bring those sensations back.

By the time she sought help, Marisol’s life had narrowed around these patterns. She had become wary in her apartment, double-checking locks and sitting with her back to the wall, and at work she was starting to step back from responsibilities that required her to be in enclosed spaces or to stay late when the building was quiet. What finally brought her in was the fear that she was no longer managing these reactions at all: the false alarms, the inability to relax even in safe places, and the creeping conviction that danger could appear anywhere had begun to govern her days. She came hoping to understand why she felt trapped long after the captivity was over, and whether there was any way to stop living as though another locked door were waiting just ahead.
